(3) Augmentation strength (H12.3): the airbench family uses translate 2 at 15 epochs (airbench95) and adds translate 4 + Cutout 12 only at 37-40 epochs (airbench96). (4) Schedule shape (H7.4): both public CIFAR-10 Muon SOTA recipes (airbench94_muon, hiverge) use plain linear decay to 0 with no warmup and no stable phase. (5) Depth cuts (H2.18): airbench95 (2 convs/block, 128/384/384, no residual) is the external 2-conv reference. The airbench paper reports that a ~20% FLOP cut (first conv per block 3x3 -> 2x2) gave no A100 wall-clock gain, the same FLOPs-don't-translate pattern as E050/E080. structured_output.summary: External evidence for the open hypotheses is mostly weak or cautionary. (1) The CIFAR-100 speedrun repos I could reach list no competing submissions with results beyond the futurebiohackers recipe (75.29% in 8.11 s) and the organizer baseline (75.36% in 59.3 s), so no external CIFAR-100 recipe exists to copy. (2) Multi-sample augmentation (H12.1, Fort et al. 2105.13343) has a real compute-matched CIFAR-100 gain, +1.6 pp at multiplicity 4, but only at 4e5 updates of bs 1024 (~8,000 epochs of samples), about 3 orders of magnitude longer than our ~7.5-epoch run. Its "fewer epochs" claim counts unique-image passes, which cost m times the compute at fixed batch size. Transfer to our regime is unsupported. (3) Augmentation strength (H12.3): the airbench family uses translate 2 at 15 epochs (airbench95) and adds translate 4 + Cutout 12 only at 37-40 epochs (airbench96). Stronger augmentation is a long-budget choice, consistent with E008. (4) Schedule shape (H7.4): both public CIFAR-10 Muon SOTA recipes (airbench94_muon, hiverge) use plain linear decay to 0 with no warmup and no stable phase. The WSD evidence I found comes from LM pretraining. The prior for WSD on a ~280-step CNN run stays low. (5) Depth cuts (H2.18): airbench95 (2 convs/block, 128/384/384, no residual) is the external 2-conv reference. The airbench paper reports that a ~20% FLOP cut (first conv per block 3x3 -> 2x2) gave no A100 wall-clock gain, the same FLOPs-don't-translate pattern as E050/E080. Profile untimed before any scored run. (6) Group-3 width (H2.19): NVIDIA's conv guide confirms the GEMM mapping (fwd N=K, dgrad N=C, wgrad M=C·R·S) and recommends channel counts divisible by 64, ideally 256. 576 = 9x64 but 2.25x256, so 512 is the cleanly aligned candidate and 640 is not. (7) New direction not in the tree: layer freezing/FreezeOut, i.e. dropping group 1 from the backward pass late in the 32 px phase. FreezeOut reports ~20% speedup without loss on WRN at 100 epochs. MosaicML's independent replication found ~5% throughput gains with accuracy losses on ImageNet and concludes it does not improve the speed/quality Pareto front. E093 also shows early-layer adaptation matters here, so the prior is low. (8) Class-balanced batches (H12.2): only generic stratified-sampling variance theory and long-tailed studies exist. No public speed recipe uses them; airbench and hiverge use plain per-epoch randperm. (9) Judge hardware: A100 80GB PCIe is 300 W vs 400 W SXM4, with slightly lower memory bandwidth (1,935 vs 2,039 GB/s per one vendor source). That supports the H2.4.3 premise that energy-bound phases slow more on the judge. Other tricks from hiverge (SiLU, selective TTA) and Fable (progressive resize, pooling, CUDA graphs) are either already tested here, refuted (SiLU, E003), or banned (TTA).

findings.claim: The only published CIFAR-100 speedrun results found are the organizer ResNet9-style baseline (40 epochs, width 64: 75.36% mean, 59.30 s on A100 80GB PCIe) and the futurebiohackers recipe (75.29% in 8.11 s on A100-SXM4). The two other forks I fetched contain no team submissions with results. The tip (~4.46 s) has no external CIFAR-100 competitor recipe to borrow from.
findings.relevance: Confirms there is no external CIFAR-100 Muon/progressive-resize recipe to mine. Remaining ideas must transfer from CIFAR-10 work or the general literature.

findings.claim: Fort et al.: at fixed batch size 1024 and equal parameter updates, CIFAR-100 WRN-16-4 with multiplicity 4 reaches 73.7±0.04% vs 72.1±0.1% for multiplicity 1 (+1.6 pp), but at 4e5 updates (~8,000 epochs of samples). Augmentations are pad + flip + random crop only. An 'epoch' is defined as one pass over the unique training set, so the claim that higher multiplicity needs fewer epochs (256 -> 128 epochs at the optimum) means m times more gradient evaluations per epoch at fixed batch size. The extracted text gives no result at budgets near ~7 sample-epochs. The authors attribute the gain to augmentation variance harming generalization.
findings.relevance: H12.1.1 halves unique-image coverage in the 32 px phase of a ~7.5-epoch run. The only compute-matched evidence is ~1000x longer, where coverage is not a constraint. The mechanism is plausible, but the regime transfer is unsupported, so keep H12.1's prior low. Our run already reduces augmentation variance through alternating flip.

findings.claim: airbench95 (15 epochs, bs 1024, LS 0.2) uses translate 2 + alternating flip with 2-conv groups at widths 128/384/384. airbench96 (37 epochs, bs 1024, LS 0.2, widths 128/384/512, 3 convs per group with residual over the last two) raises translate to 4 and adds Cutout 12. The airbench paper does not ablate translate 2 vs 4 at short budgets. It notes that alternating flip's speedup grows with training length and that Cutout partly closes the gap between random and alternating flip.
findings.relevance: Stronger geometric augmentation appears only in the 37-40-epoch recipe, consistent with E008 (more augmentation hurt at 8 epochs). This is weak evidence against H12.3.1 (translate 4 in the 28/32 px phases at ~4 epochs of late training).

findings.claim: Both public CIFAR-10 Muon SOTA recipes use a plain linear LR decay from the initial value to 0 over total steps (lr = initial*(1 - step/total)), with no warmup and no stable or WSD phase, for Muon and SGD groups alike. The whitening bias decays linearly to 0 over its own shorter window. Batches come from a uniform per-epoch randperm with no class balancing and one augmentation draw per image.
findings.relevance: No CNN speedrun evidence supports a WSD shape under Muon (H7.4). The WSD support I found comes from LM pretraining. Separately, these tuned recipes run without warmup, while E051 found halving warmup cost ~0.2 pp (noise-level). The warmup question is not resolved either way. H12.2 (stratified batches) has no precedent in any speed recipe.

findings.claim: Keller Jordan's airbench paper: 'we can lower the FLOPs of airbench96 by almost 20% by reducing the kernel size of the first convolution in each block from 3 to 2 and increasing epochs from 40 to 45. But this does not improve the wallclock training time on an A100.' airbench95 is airbench94 with 2 convs per block at widths 128/384/384. airbench96 adds a third conv per block with a residual over the last two (widths 128/512/512 in the paper). On CIFAR-100, airbench96 reaches 79.27% (79.76% with Cutout) at ~40 epochs. The paper has no isolated depth ablation.
findings.relevance: This is direct external evidence that architectural FLOP cuts on this network family can fail to reduce A100 wall time, matching E050/E080 (width cuts recovered 33-60% of FLOP-proportional time). It supports H2.18.1's 'profile untimed first' gate. It also lowers the prior that a 1-conv residual branch saves close to proportional time. The airbench95 structure is the external reference for a 2-conv-per-group variant.

findings.claim: Implicit-GEMM mapping: forward M=N·P·Q, N=K, K=C·R·S. Dgrad M=N·H·W, N=C, K=K·R·S. Wgrad M=C·R·S, N=K, K=N·P·Q, and for wgrad tile quantization 'considers only the C dimension'. Guidance: channels divisible by 8 (FP16), and batch size and channel counts 'divisible by at least 64 and ideally 256' for efficient tiling. Small equivalent GEMMs show large quantization cliffs.
findings.relevance: For H2.19: 576 = 9x64 = 2.25x256, so under 256-wide tiles group 3 already pays for 768, and 512 (2x256) is the clean alignment. 640 = 2.5x256 is not aligned, so 'widening to 640 is near-free' depends on cuDNN picking 128-wide N tiles. Reading the logged kernel names, as H2.19.1's free step says, is the right first move. If they show 64-wide tiles, close the line.

findings.claim: FreezeOut freezes layers progressively from the first one (cubic schedule, t0=0.8 before cubing, i.e. 0.512, with per-layer cosine LR annealing to 0 and LR scaled by 1/t_i), removing them from the backward pass. On CIFAR-10/100 at 100 epochs it reports ~20% wall-clock savings without accuracy loss for WRN40-4, up to 20% savings with ~3% relative error increase for DenseNet, and no benefit for VGG. The authors suggest residual or dense skips are needed.
findings.relevance: This is a new time lever the tree has not considered. Late in the 32 px phase (after ~70-80% of samples), stop backprop into group 1, skipping its wgrad/dgrad, its BN backward and the stem backward. Group 1 has the largest activation traffic (31x31x128). In this energy-bound phase that could save ~5-10% of 32 px step energy, and it is a FLOP/byte lever that should transfer to the 300 W judge. It requires an extra static graph variant warmed up in build.

findings.claim: MosaicML's layer-freezing method card: ResNet-50/ImageNet gets ~5% more throughput but loses 0.5-1% accuracy. ResNet-56/CIFAR-100 went 75.82% -> 76.22% at ~5% speedup (one unreplicated run). Their conclusion: 'There is No Evidence that Layer Freezing Improves the Tradeoff Between Model Quality and Training Speed.' They recommend freeze_start >= 0.1.
findings.relevance: This independent replication lowers the prior for the FreezeOut lever above. With E093 (early whitening-bias freeze: -0.44 pp) showing that early layers still adapt here, a group-1 freeze must be very late (e.g. the last 20-30% of the 32 px phase). It would also need to beat the measured ~0.065 pp per 1% exchange rate. Run an untimed profile of the saving first.

findings.claim: hiverge's CIFAR-10 record (2.59 -> 1.99 s) combined a vectorized/batched optimizer, a compiled train step, vectorized crops plus per-batch brightness/contrast jitter, GELU -> SiLU, SVD-based whitening init, hyperparameter retuning, and selective TTA. No per-trick gains are given. Fable's legitimate gain was mainly progressive resizing 24 -> 28 -> 32 (~7.6%, 1.98 -> 1.828 s) plus pooling, CUDA-graph and optimizer-fusion changes. Its flagged gaming tricks were precomputed augmented batches in untimed setup (~0.15 s), machine lottery and thermal cooldown.
findings.relevance: Every legitimate trick listed is already banked or refuted here (SiLU E003, brightness/contrast E008, graphs E052/E053, pooling E056). TTA and moving augmentation into build are banned by RULES. This confirms the CIFAR-10 SOTA bag of tricks is exhausted for this tree, with one cheap leftover: SVD vs eigh whitening init, which is numerically equivalent and not a lever.

findings.claim: The A100 80GB PCIe has a 300 W TDP vs 400 W for SXM4. Per the vendor comparison, memory bandwidth is ~1,935 vs ~2,039 GB/s. Peak clocks and tensor throughput are nominally the same, so sustained-load differences come from the power envelope.
findings.relevance: This supports H2.4.3's premise. The 32 px phase is energy-bound at 400 W (E045), so it will throttle harder on the 300 W judge, and FLOP/byte levers (e.g. a late group-1 freeze, depth cuts) should transfer better than per-step levers. Use it as a tie-breaker, as H2.4.3 proposes, not as a scoring signal.

findings.claim: Stratified minibatch sampling lowers the variance of the minibatch gradient estimator in theory (Zhao & Zhang 2014, clustered strata). The empirical work I found on class-balanced batch sampling targets long-tailed CIFAR-100-LT, not balanced CIFAR-100 at very short budgets.
findings.relevance: H12.2 has only generic theoretical support and no short-budget balanced-data evidence. Combined with no speed recipe using it, the prior stays at ~0.1-0.15. It is cheap (zero time cost) but should be ranked below H8.2/H2.19.
